LIBI is currently in the process of finalizing text for new exhibits to be installed in a new visitor center. In accordance with this review, staff at the park and HFC reviewed text and compared text with the Secretarial Order 3431 through ChatGPT. See below the three flagged areas:

1. Sentences: "Agitated by defeat, the US Government implemented harsher policies and broke more promise" and "The United State was hungry for land and gold." LIBI can change the text regarding "agitated", "broke more promises", and "hungry" if review board finds this language subjective.

2. "Residential US Federal Indian Boarding Schools and their commissioned Christian-based Indian Boarding schools violently erased cultural identities and language in the children they were entrusted to educated." LIBI would like to maintain this text in the exhibits as "violently erased" was language specifically requested and suggested through tribal consultation and accurately describes conditions of boarding schools as supported by the Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative - Investigative Reported that was completed in 2024.

Per requested by the Regional Director, LIBI is submitting the full content package for the new exhibits to be installed in the new visitor center in 2026. The current package is Design Development Phase #3 (DD3). DD3 has already been delievered for review and feedback received from all affiliate Tribes and stakeholders. Harper Ferry Center and the design contractor, Design Minds, are currently in the process of synthesizing and applying comments received to the final design package before fabrication. This final Design Development will be delivered towards to the end of the summer (DD4) for final park comments and review. 

Due to file sizes, all materials related to the design/text of exhibits for review are linked to NPGallery. See linked URL below. 

They include: 

1. Graphics Book - A visual representation of each display concept.
2. DD3 Text Level 3 - All panel text in full, providing a complete view of exhibit narratives.
3. AV Program Production - Concepts for four audio listening stations.
4. DD3 Content Specialties Report - Suggested artifacts and replicas for the exhibits.

Two documents have also been uploaded that track feedback from Tribal Consultation related to DD3. 

1. LIBI Consolidated DD3 Comments and Responses: Includes both comments from Tribal memebers and stakeholders. 
2. LIBI Tribal Consultation Notes 12022024: A section of this consultation was specific to exhibit design. 

The park has engaged Tribal Nations and stakeholders throughout the design process, incorporating feedback into the desing and text. The uploaded documents just relate the most recent design (DD3), but the park could provide additional information regarding past consultation for earlier design phases.

items.descriptionChanges:
The attached images are from exhibit panels and waysides at the Kingsley Plantation which may be in conflict with SO 3431 or EO 14253. The site interprets the history of slavery in Florida. 

Many images depict the torture of the enslaved women by colonial men; depict the horrid conditions the enslaved endured during their transport to the Americas; depict artifacts, like ankle racks, which were used to torture the enslaved at Kingsley Plantation; depict images of enslaved women having their children forcibly removed by men of a different color; show images of enslaved men and children in chains alongside men with brandishing whips; show images of torture scars on the backs of the enslaved; and images women and children being tortured by men with a different complexion with a cattle whip.

Certain text on the exhibits or waysides may be disparaging towards the U.S. Some text describes the horrid conditions the enslaved endured during their transport to the Americas; certain panels discuss the differences between slavery in Spanish Florida and the United States; panels discuss the race discrimiation laws that were passed once Spanish Florida became part of the U.S.; exhibits have excerpts from Zepheniah Kingsley's treatise on Florida slavery vs American slavery; waysides which discuss the misery of slavery and the unrelenting conditions suffered by the enslaved at Kingsley Plantation, how they were treated as possesions without any rights and their dehumanization. 

The park has an audio tour of the plantation grounds, which is immersive and professionally narrated. Visitors can access the tour online, but we also have preloaded audio devices that we issue for use on the grounds to folks without internet access.

Inside the museum and visitor center at Fort Caroline National Memorial, there are just a few things that need to be reviewed. 

The first is an image of a slave ship. One can see how cramped the conditions were and the text reads, "African people were brought to the new world under extreme conditions, then forced to live as slaves." 

There is text that reads, "...wetlands also contirubte to our dwindling water supply taxed by drought, waste, overuse, and increasing demands from overpopulation." 

Ther is addtional text taht reads, "If today's growing populations and advances in technology go unchecked, little of the Florida landscape will remain untouched."
Exhibit describes "Marine Debris" that collects on Biscayne National Park islands which may "emphasizes matters unrelated to the beauty, abundance, or grandeur..."

The text of this exhibit which states "After his wife, Olive, died from injuries sustained from a fall at Boca Chita in 1939, Honeywell halted his plans to further develop the island"  may not be historically accurate in that there are differing reports on the cause and location of Olive Honeywell's death.

These two wayside exhibits mention "Spite Highway" and it has been brought to our attention recently at least one individual believes the name "maligns the Elliott Key property owners who did not build a road out of ‘spite."
